difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — two directly linked concepts (area of a regular dodecagon from its triangles, then assembling a square from the pieces) with a few routine steps; about 2–3 minutes.
stem:
A regular dodecagon (12-sided regular polygon) is inscribed in a circle of radius $r$ cm as shown in the figure. The side of the dodecagon is $d$ cm. All the triangles (numbered 1 to 12) in the figure are used to form squares of side $r$ cm and each numbered triangle is used only once to form a square.

The number of squares that can be formed and the number of triangles required to form each square, respectively, are:

Note: The figure shown is representative.

![Figure: A regular dodecagon inscribed in a dashed circle and divided into 12 numbered triangles. Triangles 1, 4 and 7 join the centre to two vertices two steps apart; triangles 2, 3, 5, 6, 8 and 9 join the centre to the two ends of one dodecagon side; triangles 10, 11 and 12 are the thin triangles between the outer sides of triangles 1, 4, 7 and the two dodecagon sides beyond them. One dodecagon side (next to triangle 3) is labelled d.](/pyq/2025/fig/Q08-1.png)

solution.quick: A regular dodecagon inscribed in a circle of radius $r$ has area $12 \times \tfrac12 r^2 \sin 30^\circ = 3r^2$, exactly three squares of side $r$. The 12 triangles split evenly, so each square uses $12 \div 3 = 4$ triangles: one equilateral triangle, two $30^\circ$ isosceles triangles and one thin cap triangle. Answer **(A)** 3; 4.

steps.title: Classify the 12 triangles
steps.body:
Let $O$ be the centre; the dodecagon’s vertices are $30^\circ$ apart on the circle. A chord subtending a central angle $\theta$ has length $2r\sin(\theta/2)$, so a $60^\circ$ chord has length $r$ and a $30^\circ$ chord has length $d = 2r\sin 15^\circ \approx 0.518r$.

| Type | Triangles | Description | Sides | Area |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E | 1, 4, 7 | centre + two vertices $60^\circ$ apart | $r, r, r$ (equilateral) | $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}r^2 \approx 0.433r^2$ |
| I | 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9 | centre + two adjacent vertices ($30^\circ$ apart) | $r, r, d$ | $\frac12 r^2\sin30^\circ = \frac{r^2}{4}$ |
| C | 10, 11, 12 | cap between two sides $d$ and a chord $r$ | $d, d, r$ (apex $150^\circ$) | $2\cdot\frac{r^2}{4} - \frac{\sqrt3}{4}r^2 \approx 0.067r^2$ |

(The area of a cap C is the area of two type-I triangles minus the equilateral triangle that shares the same chord.)

steps.title: Total area of the dodecagon
steps.body:
$$3\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{4}r^2 + 6\cdot\frac{r^2}{4} + 3\left(\frac{r^2}{2} - \frac{\sqrt3}{4}r^2\right) = \frac{3}{2}r^2 + \frac{3}{2}r^2 = 3r^2.$$

Check: the dodecagon is also 12 central triangles of angle $30^\circ$, i.e. $12 \times \frac{r^2}{4} = 3r^2$.

steps.title: Number of squares and triangles per square
steps.body:
Each square of side $r$ has area $r^2$, and every triangle is used exactly once, so the number of squares is

$$\frac{3r^2}{r^2} = 3.$$

No single triangle, pair or triple of these triangles has total area exactly $r^2$: the largest pair is $E+E \approx 0.866r^2$, and the triples give $1.299, 1.116, 0.933, 0.933, 0.750, 0.750, 0.567, 0.567, 0.384, 0.201$ (in units of $r^2$). So each square needs at least 4 triangles, and with only 12 triangles for 3 squares, each square uses **exactly 4**.

steps.title: Show that a square really can be assembled
steps.body:
Take a square $ABCD$ of side $r$ and build the equilateral triangle $ABP$ on side $AB$, inside the square (type E).

- $AP = AD = r$ and $\angle PAD = 90^\circ - 60^\circ = 30^\circ$, so $\triangle APD$ has sides $r, r, d$: type I. Likewise $\triangle BPC$ is type I.
- The base angles of each type-I triangle are $75^\circ$, so the angle of the remaining $\triangle DPC$ at $P$ is $360^\circ - 60^\circ - 75^\circ - 75^\circ = 150^\circ$, with $PD = PC = d$ and $DC = r$: type C.

Area check: $\frac{\sqrt3}{4} + \frac14 + \frac14 + \left(\frac12 - \frac{\sqrt3}{4}\right) = 1$ (units of $r^2$). The pieces available are exactly 3 of type E, 6 of type I and 3 of type C, which make three such squares: each takes one of {1, 4, 7}, two of {2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9} and one of {10, 11, 12}.

(Other groups of four also have area $r^2$ — two E with two C, or four I — but they cannot tile a square: a square’s corner of $90^\circ$ would need $60^\circ + 15^\circ + 15^\circ$ or $30^\circ + 30^\circ + 30^\circ$ at every corner, and those groups do not have enough $15^\circ$ or $30^\circ$ angles. Either way the count is 4 triangles per square.)

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: 3 squares can be formed, each from 4 triangles: **(A) 3; 4**.

solution.teaching:
**Area is conserved when shapes are cut and reassembled.** Whatever you build from a set of pieces has exactly the total area of those pieces. So in any ‘use all the pieces to form squares’ problem, first compute the total area; the number of squares is fixed by it. Then check that the pieces can actually be fitted together, using side lengths and angles.

**Area of a regular polygon inscribed in a circle.** Join the centre to every vertex. A regular $n$-gon splits into $n$ congruent isosceles triangles with two sides $r$ and apex angle $\frac{360^\circ}{n}$. Using area $= \frac12 ab\sin C$,

$$\text{Area} = n \cdot \frac12 r^2 \sin\frac{360^\circ}{n}.$$

For $n = 12$: $12 \cdot \frac12 r^2 \sin 30^\circ = 3r^2$, a classical and easy-to-remember result (Kürschák’s tile is a well-known dissection proof of it). Compare this with the circle’s area $\pi r^2 \approx 3.14r^2$: the dodecagon fills almost all of the circle.

**Chord lengths.** A chord subtending central angle $\theta$ has length $2r\sin(\theta/2)$. For $\theta = 60^\circ$ this is exactly $r$, which is why triangles 1, 4 and 7 are equilateral with side $r$ — the same as the side of the target square. That is the hint that each square is built around one equilateral triangle, with two narrow $30^\circ$ triangles on its sides and a thin $150^\circ$ cap filling the last gap.

In this question, area gives 3 squares, and because no fewer than 4 of the given triangles can add up to area $r^2$, the 12 triangles must be shared 4 per square.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: The dodecagon’s area is $3r^2$, giving 3 squares of area $r^2$; the 12 triangles split 4 per square (one equilateral, two $30^\circ$ isosceles, one cap), and such a square can be assembled exactly.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Four squares would need total area $4r^2$, but all 12 triangles together have area only $3r^2$ (less even than the circle’s $\pi r^2$).

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Three squares of 3 triangles would use only 9 of the 12 triangles, contradicting ‘all the triangles are used’; moreover no three of these triangles have total area exactly $r^2$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Three squares of 2 triangles would use only 6 triangles; and no two of these triangles can make area $r^2$ (the largest pair, two equilateral triangles, has area $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}r^2 \approx 0.866r^2$).

solution.shortcut: Remember that a regular dodecagon inscribed in a circle of radius $r$ has area exactly $3r^2$. So 3 squares of side $r$, and $12 \div 3 = 4$ triangles each.
solution.commonTrap: Overlooking the thin cap triangles 10, 11 and 12 and building each square from only the big central triangles (one equilateral + two narrow ones), which suggests ‘3; 3’. Those three pieces have area only $\approx 0.933r^2$; the cap is needed to complete each square.

answerVerification.checkCode:
import sympy as sp
from itertools import combinations_with_replacement as cwr, combinations
from collections import Counter
# r = 1. E = centre + vertices 60 deg apart (1,4,7); I = centre + adjacent vertices (2,3,5,6,8,9); C = thin cap (10,11,12)
E=sp.sqrt(3)/4; I=sp.sin(sp.pi/6)/2; C=2*I-E; area={'E':E,'I':I,'C':C}
total=sp.nsimplify(3*E+6*I+3*C); print('dodecagon area =',total,'-> squares of side r:',total)
combos={k:[c for c in cwr('EIC',k) if sp.simplify(sum(area[p] for p in c)-1)==0] for k in (1,2,3,4)}
print('piece-multisets with area exactly r^2:',combos)
# necessary condition for tiling a square: the 4 right-angle corners must each be filled by piece angles summing to 90
ang={'E':[60,60,60],'I':[30,75,75],'C':[150,15,15]}
def fill(k,pool):
    if k==0: return True
    items=sorted(pool.elements())
    return any(fill(k-1,pool-Counter(s)) for r in (1,2,3) for s in set(combinations(items,r)) if sum(s)==90)
print('corner-feasible 4-piece combos:',[c for c in combos[4] if fill(4,Counter(a for p in c for a in ang[p]))])
# explicit assembly E+I+I+C: square ABCD, equilateral ABP inside
d=2*sp.sin(sp.pi/12); P=sp.Matrix([sp.Rational(1,2),sp.sqrt(3)/2]); A,B,Cc,D=[sp.Matrix(p) for p in [(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)]]
L=lambda X,Y: sp.sqrt(((X-Y).T*(X-Y))[0])
print('PD-d, PC-d, AP-1, BP-1:',[sp.simplify(x) for x in (L(P,D)-d,L(P,Cc)-d,L(A,P)-1,L(B,P)-1)])
answerVerification.notes: Blind re-solve (before viewing the key): dodecagon area $=12\cdot\tfrac12 r^2\sin30^\circ=3r^2$ → 3 squares of area $r^2$; 12 triangles / 3 squares = 4 per square; explicit tiling = 1 equilateral (1, 4 or 7) + two $30^\circ$ isosceles (2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9) + one $150^\circ$ cap (10, 11, 12) → (A) 3; 4, agreeing with the official key A. The sympy check confirms total area 3, that no 1, 2 or 3 pieces have area exactly $r^2$, that the 4-piece multisets with area $r^2$ are E+E+C+C, E+I+I+C and I+I+I+I, that only E+I+I+C passes the necessary corner-angle test (four $90^\circ$ corners filled by piece angles), and the side lengths of the explicit E+I+I+C square. Verifier additions: a note in Step 4 on why the other area-$r^2$ groups cannot tile a square; the Kürschák’s-tile remark was reworded.
